author: Independent education critic subagent (claude-opus-5-5); did not author the reviewed artifacts

findings.claim: The coverage plan misstates which objectives the final MCQ leaves out. Section 5 names three (generics#o1, stacks-and-queues#o3, timed-coding-screen-patterns#o2), but the blueprint objectives list 36 of the 42 taught objectives. It also leaves out choosing-the-right-collection#o2 (ArrayList over LinkedList by documented cost), the-equals-and-hashcode-contract#o1 (state the equals contract) and wrapper-types-and-autoboxing#o1 (identify where boxing happens). All three can be assessed by MCQ. Every topic still maps to at least one planned question, so topic-level coverage holds.
findings.recommendation: Either fold the three into existing items (choosing#o2 into q09, equals#o1 into q07, wrapper#o1 into q05) and add them to the blueprint's objectives and objectiveFormats, or list all six omissions with honest reasons in section 5.

findings.claim: 15 items in 15 minutes is not a credible fit for the plan as written. Every item is described as multi-step with code (tracing, debugging from a symptom, predicting a transformation), and q13 (laziness, reuse failure and SQL-versus-stream placement) and q15 (pattern recognition, Big-O and an empty-result bug) pack three or four objectives into one item, which is well over 60 seconds of reading and reasoning for a beginner. The plan flags this risk but leaves the decision to the private author, so the learner-facing promise '15 questions in 15 minutes' ships unresolved.
findings.recommendation: Decide now and record it in the blueprint and plan: either make hard authoring constraints (snippet of 8 lines or fewer, at most two objectives per item, q13 and q15 reduced to one decision each), or adopt the plan's 12-item / 15-minute fallback with the topic map re-checked. Ask the private author to time each item on a pilot reader and record 'timed at <commit>' without values.

findings.claim: objectiveFormats credits three or four objectives to single 4-option items (q09, q12, q13, q14, q15). One keyed response cannot show mastery of four separate objectives; for example, a correct q15 answer cannot show both recognising the pattern and spotting the bug. Reporting by objective will overstate the evidence.
findings.recommendation: In the coverage plan, give each planned item one primary objective for reporting and list the others as context. Make sure every taught topic still has at least one item where its objective is primary.

findings.claim: The course owner asked for a final that steps up in difficulty. The plan shows step-up only against the practice banks ('new and harder'). It records no difficulty level per item and no ordering principle: items follow syllabus order, and single-topic and cross-topic items are mixed throughout. A reviewer cannot check the step-up claim.
findings.recommendation: Add a column to the section 4 table giving each item's cognitive level (apply / analyze / evaluate) and whether it is single- or cross-topic, and state the intended order (for example, single-topic tracing first, cross-topic diagnosis and design last).

findings.claim: The learner instructions are clear about count, time, item types and pass mark, and contain no protected values. But they are one long paragraph with internal labels ('Day F28', 'the 15-minute multiple-choice part of the F28 module check'), and they send mixed signals: 'the course's one graded, cumulative multiple-choice assessment' versus 'part of the module check', with the practical 'separate'. The first allowedResources entry (line 163) is author jargon ('The frozen calendar states no AI or resource rule for the F28 Module check block').
findings.recommendation: Use four short sentences: what it is (the graded final quiz that ends the Course Review), its size (15 questions, 15 minutes, covering every topic), the question types (many combine two topics), and the pass mark (70%) and where resource rules appear. Drop the calendar ids. Rephrase allowedResources as 'Your assessment platform shows which resources you may use.'

findings.claim: The differentiation list is generic, so specific collisions are left for the private author to find. Three stand out. q09 ('choose an implementation for several stated needs at once') has the same shape as Activity 1 of the review scenarios page taken minutes earlier. q05 (a counting map that fails on an unseen key) sits close to the wrapper-types GIFT item on unboxing a missing map value and to coding Task 1 of the same module check, which counts with merge or getOrDefault. q10 and q14 mirror coding Task 2 (two-key Comparator; grouping where keys repeat).
findings.recommendation: Name these collisions in section 6. Give q09 a different decision dimension, such as a conflict between operation cost and order guarantee, and make sure q05, q10 and q14 do not preview the coding practical's exact tasks.
